We need a holistic plan, but look, at the height of the Great Recession in 2009, we passed the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act, and that helped prevent large increases in poverty by increasing the maximum SNAP benefit by 13.5 or 13.6%, totaling to about $1.74 per per meal. Look, that's not a lot, but what we're doing in this bill is we're increasing the SNAP benefit by 15%. And, look, I mean, I've been on the Agriculture Committee for a long time on the Nutrition Subcommittee and, you know, the couple of things that I I've learned is that one is that some of the people who are the biggest critics of the program know nothing about the program. I have colleagues who I'm not even sure I ever talk to anybody who's on SNAP. I have a lot of colleagues who don't know what the average SNAP benefit is. And I have colleagues who come up with the old tired refrain every time we talk about trying to improve the program when they say, well, just have them go get a job. Again, I remind them that the majority of people who can work, who are on SNAP, actually do work. So, you know, we need to get beyond the, you know, the title, political talking points have been used to do nothing and understand that this is a huge, huge problem. And again, it's not just about the SNAP program. We have to improve that program and we have to increase the benefits, but it is about much, much, much more. And by the way, as we're doing this, we also need to pay attention to the issue of nutrition. So, yeah, we want to make sure that people are not food insecure. We also want to make sure people have access to nutritious food. Because, you know, we don't want to solve one problem, only to create another problem. So, you know, providing people food that's not nutritious, you know, again, results in healthcare challenges that, quite frankly, are very costly. increase suffering amongst individuals.
